newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia hopes to end corn imports by 1999.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia hopes to end corn imports by 1999.

text.p: Indonesia aims to end corn imports by 1999 with the introduction of high-yield U.S. strains and a ground-breaking purchase agreement between feedmillers and local farmers, an industry official said on Thursday.

Budiarto Soebijanto, chairman of the Federation of Indonesian Feedmillers (GPMT), said some 50,000 hectares (124,000 acres) would be planted with the U.S. hybrid, which yields about four times more corn than the two tonnes per hectare (2.5 acres) produced by local varieties.
He said about 30 feedmillers had signed agreements with farmers through state-backed cooperatives to buy their corn, guaranteeing them a minimum of 320 rupiah (U.S. 14 cents) per kg.
"The first series of contracts were signed last month and fresh contracts are expected to be signed every month," he told Reuters. "This is the first such collective signing of contracts."
He said the contracts were aimed at keeping farmers from abandoning corn for other crops.
Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country with nearly 200 million people, takes pride in its rice self-sufficiency and hopes to emulate that feat with other crops, starting with corn.
To expand crop cultivation outside the densely-populated main island of Java, where two-thirds of the population resides, government policies encourage families on Java to relocate to other islands.

The Jakarta office of the U.S. Feed Grains Council last week released figures indicating that Indonesia's corn imports are unlikely to grow significantly this year. It said about 665,000 tonnes of corn were imported in the first nine months of 1996, against 1,087,813 tonnes for all of last year.
Grain traders said 1996 imports were expected to exceed one million tonnes but added that increased local supply would significantly reduce imports before the turn of the century.
According to official data, local corn output rose by 19.7 percent to 8.2 million tonnes in 1995 over the previous year and was cultivated on 3.23 million hectares (eight million acres).
"There's a lot of interest being generated by the planting of the hybrid varieties and the signing of the purchasing contracts by feedmillers," one trader said.

"There are strong signals that output is going to increase substantially in the coming years," he said. "But to ensure the success of the hybrid planting, local prices must be attractive enough for the farmers not to switch to other crops."
Traders said the 50,000 hectares being planted with the hybrid varieties could boost production by an additional 200,000 tonnes every three months.
"Even if there were only three harvests a year, we would see an increase of 600,000 tonnes of corn annually," another trader said.
"But I think the hybrid project will take two to three years to get on a firm footing as things like fertiliser supply have to be sustained and prices, too, must be attractive," he added.
